This page covers the precise US O*NET/SOC 11-3051.06 occupation "Hydroelectric Production Managers": managing operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities and maintaining and monitoring hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Original official scope: Manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities. Maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. US wage and employment data on this page come from BLS OEWS for 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 as presented by O*NET, which labels both datasets as combined figures for Industrial Production Managers. Precise occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap. The jurisdictions and safety systems on the two sides cannot be applied interchangeably.

To assess whether hydroelectric production management suits you, first carry out a verifiable management exercise using public or simulated materials. Set up a fictional plant operating scenario, such as an unplanned unit shutdown with environmental containment requirements. Write a step-by-step process covering confirmation of operating status and impacts; organization of shift and maintenance resources; identification and communication of system emergencies; development and approval of response and recovery plans; supervision of safety compliance, containment and cleanup; and restoration of generation and reporting to management. For each step, identify the grounds for judgment, matters requiring instructions or approval, and possible exceptions: escalation of the emergency, insufficient staffing or spare parts, conflicts between the plan and safety or compliance, expansion of the environmental incident, and inconsistent communication among parties. Afterwards, check whether safety compliance, containment and environmental protection, and work permits are treated as indispensable; whether matters beyond personal authority or requiring external approval are submitted for instructions; and whether decision grounds and actions are recorded for review. Test this through actual deliverables rather than answers based solely on an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | US O*NET 11-3051.06 work activities show that communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates; making decisions and solving problems; inspecting equipment, structures or materials; documenting information; organizing, planning and prioritizing; and coordinating others' work are the most important activities in this occupation. Work context responses show: email 100% indicates daily; telephone conversations 98% indicates daily; responsibility for other workers' health and safety 85% indicates very high; face-to-face discussions 83% indicates daily; wearing common protective or safety equipment 77% indicates daily; responsibility for others' work outcomes 64% indicates very high; typical workweek 65% indicates more than 40 hours; freedom to make decisions 60% indicates considerable freedom; and consequences of error 48% indicates extremely serious. The most important skills include active listening, speaking, monitoring, reading comprehension and critical thinking. Judgment and decision making, management of personnel resources, time management and complex problem solving rank highly among transferable skills. If you are willing to coordinate people and operations amid equipment and safety risks and take responsibility for outcomes and safety, these daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (11-3051.06): responsibility for other workers' health and safety 85% indicates very high; wearing common protective or safety equipment 77% indicates daily; responsibility for others' work outcomes 64% indicates very high; typical workweek 65% indicates more than 40 hours; exposure to noise 49% indicates daily; outdoor exposure to all weather conditions 54% indicates once a week or more; exposure to hazardous conditions 32% indicates daily; and consequences of error 48% indicates extremely serious. This occupation concerns hydroelectric facilities, rotating and energized equipment, plant safety and environmental compliance. A delay in judging or reporting an emergency, a lapse in work permit or isolation oversight, delayed containment and cleanup, or an incorrect compliance judgment may cause personal injury, equipment damage, interruption of electricity supply or an environmental accident. This page therefore separately addresses safety compliance and work permit oversight, equipment and emergency response, environmental protection and containment, and authority and approval boundaries. The occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook in the US. The O*NET page shows that the related combined category, Industrial Production Managers, is projected to grow below average (2%) in 2024–2034, with approximately 17,100 annual job openings and approximately 241,900 people employed in 2024. These are combined figures for Industrial Production Managers, not the precise size of this occupation. If safety and compliance responsibility, long hours or emergency pressure are difficult for you to bear, treat them as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Judging responsibility | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same operating decision: make operations effective by confirming operating status, organizing people and resources, overseeing equipment maintenance and repairs, planning production to meet customer needs, and producing reviewable operating and maintenance records; manage safety, compliance and environmental protection by overseeing isolation, tagging and work permits, identifying and communicating emergencies, and performing or directing containment and cleanup in accordance with institutional and regulatory requirements; and assume defined management responsibility for operating outcomes, team performance and safety compliance, seeking instructions under established procedures for matters beyond your authority or requiring external approval. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as producing a step-by-step operating process and decision record or rehearsing identification and handling of common emergency and compliance situations, rather than relying only on interest questionnaire conclusions.

The daily work of hydroelectric production managers can be divided into three strands: (1) operations and resources—confirm operating status, organize shift and maintenance resources, and plan production to meet demand; (2) safety and compliance—oversee isolation, tagging and work permits, identify and communicate emergencies, and inspect facilities for compliance with safety standards and regulations; (3) environmental protection and records—perform or direct containment and cleanup, maintain operating and maintenance records, and report to management and dispatch. All three strands share the same safety and compliance requirements, but their outputs differ: operations concern generation and equipment availability; safety and compliance concern risk control; environmental protection and records concern compliance and the chain of accountability.

O*NET 11-3051.06, "Hydroelectric Production Managers": manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities and maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Core tasks include directing operations, maintenance and repairs; identifying and communicating system emergencies; maintaining operating and maintenance records; performing or directing containment and cleanup; monitoring or inspecting equipment and facilities; overseeing compliance with regulations and standards; and planning and coordinating production operations. Job Zone Three (medium preparation required).

Hydroelectric production managers (O*NET/SOC 11-3051.06, "Hydroelectric Production Managers") are managers who manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities and maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Original official scope: Manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities. Maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Core tasks are directing operations, maintenance or repairs at hydroelectric facilities; identifying and communicating power system emergencies; maintaining operating, maintenance or repair records; performing or directing preventive and corrective containment or cleanup to protect the environment; monitoring or inspecting equipment such as turbines, generators or control systems; inspecting facilities such as switchyards, control rooms and relay rooms to ensure normal operation or compliance with safety standards; overseeing operations to ensure that generating or mechanical equipment complies with applicable regulations or standards; and planning or coordinating hydroelectric production operations to meet customer needs. Common job titles include Hydroelectric Station Supervisor, Plant Manager, Power Plant Superintendent, Power Plant Supervisor and Power Project Manager. subject.name: Hydroelectric Production Managers
subject.summary: Hydroelectric production managers correspond to the precise US O*NET/SOC 11-3051.06 occupation, "Hydroelectric Production Managers": they manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities and maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Original official scope: Manage operations at hydroelectric power generation facilities. Maintain and monitor hydroelectric plant equipment for efficient and safe plant operations. Core tasks include directing operations, maintenance and repairs; identifying and communicating system emergencies; maintaining operating and maintenance records; performing or directing containment and cleanup; monitoring or inspecting equipment and facilities; overseeing compliance with regulations and standards; and planning and coordinating production operations. US wage and employment data on this page come from BLS OEWS for 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 as presented by O*NET, which labels both datasets as combined figures for Industrial Production Managers. Precise occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap; Chinese qualification and work safety systems boundaries are identified separately.
